abstract.value: Agent skills are a natural substrate for continual learning in large language model agents because they allow useful procedural knowledge to be loaded only when needed rather than kept in context at all times, which support progressive disclosure of external experience and tools. However,  practical skill learning still faces two coupled challenges: skills must keep evolving from execution-time experience to adapt to tasks, and, once large numbers of new skills are appended, there is no effective governance mechanism that respects the unique properties of skills as reusable procedural objects. In this paper, we introduce **EvoSkillBank**, a controlled continual skill learning framework that enables agents to self-evolve skills from benchmark interaction traces while maintaining a persistent and governed SkillBank. EvoSkillBank combines a test-time self-evolution process for turning raw trajectories into reusable skill candidates with a SkillBank evolution framework that regulates how newly generated skills are added, merged, deprecated, or rejected. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, QA show that EvoSkillBank consistently improves over direct inference and static skill repositories, while yielding a compact and increasingly stable SkillBank under continual growth. We release the repository for both our self-evolution framework and the governed skill storage system to support future research on controlled continual skill learning for agentic LLMs.

## Q: Multi-Backbone Evaluation of EvoSkillBank’s Model-Agnostic Gains
**Response to Reject 6 / Question 4.** Thank you for pointing this out. We added experiments with four additional base models: **Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507**, **Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507**, **GPT-4o**, and **Gemini-2.5-Pro**. For each model, we compare ReAct and EvoSkillBank under the same setting. The results show that EvoSkillBank consistently improves over ReAct across different model families and model scales, indicating that the gains are not tied to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct specifically.

For ReAct, 
| Model | Pick | Look | Clean | Heat | Cool | Pick2 | ALFWorld Avg. | WebShop Score | WebShop Succ. |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | 44.7 | 32.8 | 31.5 | 12.1 | 16.9 | 15.3 | 25.6 | 43.8 | 17.6 |
| Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 | 67.4 | 52.8 | 18.7 | 36.5 | 22.1 | 27.6 | 37.5 | 47.6 | 15.9 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 | 79.6 | 58.4 | 39.7 | 49.1 | 31.8 | 61.2 | 53.3 | 42.5 | 13.2 |
| GPT-4o | 78.9 | 60.2 | 22.4 | 53.7 | 19.6 | 38.8 | 45.6 | 31.8 | 25.9 |
| Gemini-2.5-Pro | 82.6 | 50.9 | 63.8 | 65.1 | 27.4 | 56.7 | 57.8 | 50.4 | 36.5 |

For **EvoSkillBank**, 

| Model | Pick | Look | Clean | Heat | Cool | Pick2 | ALFWorld Avg. | WebShop Score | WebShop Succ. |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | 72.8 | 64.9 | 47.6 | 39.8 | 35.4 | 30.1 | 48.4 | 61.7 | 31.5 |
| Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 | 75.9 | 58.7 | 51.6 | 53.9 | 63.8 | 38.4 | 57.1 | 50.2 | 35.7 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 | 80.7 | 75.6 | 77.9 | 80.8 | 59.6 | 55.9 | 71.8 | 57.2 | 54.9 |
| GPT-4o | 88.4 | 86.7 | 84.9 | 88.6 | 78.9 | 85.4 | 85.5 | 73.8 | 63.9 |
| Gemini-2.5-Pro | 92.7 | 91.8 | 88.6 | 84.9 | 74.8 | 91.9 | 87.5 | 80.9 | 70.8 |

These results show that EvoSkillBank provides consistent improvements across all tested backbones. The improvement is particularly clear for stronger models such as GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Pro, where ReAct already has strong reasoning and acting capability, but EvoSkillBank still improves performance by providing reusable external procedural knowledge. This suggests that EvoSkillBank is not exploiting model-specific behavior of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; instead, the SkillBank acts as a model-agnostic test-time learning substrate.

## Q: Sensitivity Analysis of the Incremental Clustering Threshold
**Response to Reject 7 / Question 5.** Thank you for pointing this out. We added a threshold sensitivity study by varying the clustering threshold used for incremental experience assignment. The results are shown below.

| Clustering Threshold | #Clusters | #Promoted Skills | ALFWorld | WebShop | Hop QA | Observation |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 0.65 | 31 | 64 | 45.9 | 58.8 | 38.6 | Over-merging; skills become too broad |
| 0.70 | 38 | 76 | 47.6 | 60.5 | 40.7 | Mild over-merging |
| 0.75 | 46 | 92 | **48.4** | **61.7** | **42.0** | Default; best overall balance |
| 0.80 | 57 | 103 | 47.9 | 61.1 | 41.4 | Stable but slightly more redundant |
| 0.85 | 73 | 128 | 46.8 | 59.6 | 39.9 | Over-fragmentation; retrieval overlap increases |

The results show that performance remains stable in the middle range from **0.70 to 0.80**, while degradation mainly appears at the two extremes. When the threshold is too low, distinct experience patterns are merged into overly broad clusters, reducing skill specificity. When the threshold is too high, similar experiences are split into many small clusters, producing redundant skills and increasing retrieval overlap. The default threshold of **0.75** was selected because it provides the best trade-off between skill specificity, repository compactness, and downstream task performance.

## Q: RegTest Subset Construction and Robustness to Sampling Seeds
**Response to Reject 8 / Question 6.** Thank you for pointing this out. We added a detailed description of the RegTest subset construction. For each benchmark, the RegTest subset is sampled from the benchmark tasks. We use stratified sampling to preserve task diversity: for ALFWorld, we sample across the six task types; for WebShop, we sample across different types; for QA, we sample across single-hop and multi-hop datasets. Importantly, the subset contains both initially successful and initially failed cases, so it does not only preserve already solved behaviors but also tests whether SkillBank updates improve or damage previously difficult cases.

| Benchmark | RegTest Size | Success / Failure Composition | Final Performance under Alternative Seeds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ALFWorld All| 60 | 30 / 30 | 48.4 ±0.9 |
| WebShop Succ.| 45 | 22 / 23 | 31.5 ±1.1 |
| QA Tasks Avg.| 140 | 70 / 70 | 42.0±1.3 |

To further check overfitting risk, we repeated the RegTest procedure with alternative subsets sampled using different random seeds. The final performance remained stable, with all variations within **1.5 points**.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the main motivation and contribution of our work, especially the shift from one-time skill construction to closed-loop SkillBank lifecycle management. We are also encouraged that the reviewer finds the ADD/UPDATE/DEPRECATE/NOOP governance mechanism, regression-based validation, and multi-benchmark evaluation practically meaningful.

## Q: Clarifying Skill Generation Models and Qwen’s Capability for Modular Skill Evolution
**Response to Weakness 1.**  Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that the model used for skill generation should be made explicit, and we will clarify this in the revised manuscript.

In our current implementation, the initial SkillBank is constructed with GPT-4o, while the self-evolution process after deployment is performed by the agent backbone itself. Although Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is a relatively small model and may show uneven performance on very long-horizon agentic tasks, we found that it is sufficiently capable for the more localized subtasks required by EvoSkillBank. The key reason is that our framework does not ask the model to solve the entire long-context continual learning problem in a single prompt. Instead, EvoSkillBank decomposes skill evolution into a sequence of fine-grained operations, such as extracting observations, identifying reusable cues, generating applicability conditions, producing action skeletons, and specifying boundary constraints. Each LLM call only needs to perform one narrowly scoped transformation over a compact trajectory or cluster representation.

## Q: Clarifying Hierarchy as a Multi-Level Method

**Response to Weakness 2.**  Thank you for raising this question. We agree that the term “hierarchical” may be ambiguous in the current manuscript, and we will clarify its meaning in the revision.

In EvoSkillBank, “hierarchical” refers to the multi-level abstraction process from agent trajectories to reusable skills, rather than to a tree-structured hierarchy inside the SkillBank. As illustrated in Figure 1, the self-evolution pipeline progressively converts raw agent trajectories into SkillBank entries through three abstraction layers: (1) experience distillation; (2) experience aggregation; and (3) skill synthesis.

Throughout this process, the intermediate representations are maintained in an object-like schema rather than as unstructured text. The finalized skill entry follows a structured schema including fields such as `title`, `principle`, `when to use`, `action skeleton`, `retrieval features`, `known failure modes`, and `guardrails`, as shown by the representative skill examples in Table 7. Therefore, the hierarchy is reflected in the progressive refinement path from trajectory-level evidence, to experience-level abstraction, to pattern-level aggregation, and finally to skill-level procedural knowledge.

We will revise the paper to make this distinction explicit: the hierarchy in EvoSkillBank is a methodological hierarchy of abstraction and refinement, not a manually defined hierarchical taxonomy within the SkillBank. 

## Q: Distinguishing EvoSkillBank from Related Work
**Response to Weakness 3.**  
Thank you for the comment. We agree that SkillRL and Skill0 are related work, but EvoSkillBank has a different focus. 

1. **SkillBank lifecycle governance.** SkillRL and Skill0 have implemented some methods for skill generation, while our EvoSkillBank focuses on how a persistent SkillBank should be maintained after skills are continuously generated. EvoSkillBank introduces explicit lifecycle governance for the SkillBank, where each candidate skill is regulated through actions such as `ADD`, `UPDATE`, `DEPRECATE`, or `NOOP`.

2. **Test-time continual learning rather than training-time learning.** SkillRL and Skill0 mainly study how skills are internalized for agentic learning. Our setting is training-free test-time continual learning. Skills are used as progressively disclosed external procedural context and refined from test-time success/failure trajectories. Thus, EvoSkillBank fills a different gap from SkillRL and Skill0: governed evolution of a growing skill repository under test-time scaling.

## Q: Adding ReasoningBank to Baseline
**Response to Weakness 4.**  Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that ReasoningBank is a relevant baseline because it also studies agent self-evolution with reusable reasoning memory. We use the ReasoningBank approach to extract success/failure experiences. This comparison is intended to isolate whether the gains come from generic reasoning-memory retrieval or from the proposed governed skill repository.

| Method | ALFWorld | WebShop | QA Tasks |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ReasoningBank | 37.6 | 53.2 | 35.8 |
| Self-Evolution | 41.8 | 56.8 | 39.4 |
| EvoSkillBank | 48.4 | 61.7 | 42.0 |

The experimental results show that ReasoningBank approach is inferior to our EvoSkillBank in both Skill generation (Self-Evolution metrics) and SkillBank governance(EvoSkillBank metrics).

## Q: Reframing Saturation as Stable Long-Horizon SkillBank Maintenance

**Response to Weakness 5.**  Thank you for this insightful observation. Our EvoSkillBank does not aim to prove unbounded capability growth. Our claim is controlled continual improvement and stable SkillBank maintenance under continual experience accumulation. The observed saturation is expected in a bounded benchmark such as ALFWorld, where reusable task patterns are finite. In fact, the slowdown of ADD operations and the increase of UPDATE/NOOP decisions indicate that the governance module prevents uncontrolled SkillBank growth. To further validate the long-horizon behavior, we extend the ALFWorld evolution analysis from iteration 5 to iteration 15. 

| Iteration | ALFWorld All | Skills in SkillBank |
|---:|---:|---:|
| **5** | **48.4** | **92** |
| 7 | 48.1 | 94 |
| 9 | 48.4 | 96 |
| 11 | 48.3 | 97 |
| 13 | 48.0 | 99 |
| 15 | 48.2 | 100 |

We found that after more than 5 iterations, it was almost impossible to obtain any gains. These results suggest that EvoSkillBank should be understood as a framework for controlled continual refinement rather than unlimited skill accumulation.

## Q: Extending Evaluation to Larger Multi-Domain Benchmarks

**Response to Weakness 6.**  Thank you for the valuable suggestion. We agree that evaluating EvoSkillBank in larger-scale multi-domain environments can better stress-test the stability of the SkillBank and the scalability of the governance module.

To address this concern, we additionally conduct experiments on WebArena and ToolBench. We use the same self-evolution setting as in the other benchmarks. The evolution process is run iteratively, and we observe that EvoSkillBank also reaches a relatively strong and stable performance around the 5th iteration on these environments.

| Method | WebArena  success rate | ToolBench pass@1 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | 8.6 | 44.6 |
| Reflexion | 16.4 | 57.1 |
| **EvoSkillBank** | **26.3** | **68.2** |

The results show that EvoSkillBank consistently outperforms both the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Reflexion baseline on WebArena and ToolBench. This suggests that the proposed SkillBank evolution mechanism is not limited to ALFWorld, WebShop, or QA tasks, but can also generalize to larger-scale multi-domain agent environments. More importantly, the stable improvement after several iterations indicates that the governance module can help maintain a useful and compact SkillBank even when the task distribution becomes broader and the skill repository grows larger.

We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback. We agree that the original submission explained the high-level idea more clearly than the concrete implementation details.

## Reproducibility and Implementation clarity

To address the concern about engineering choices, we will add a step-by-step implementation description of EvoSkillBank. In our implementation, the governance mechanism is instantiated as a mostly deterministic pipeline, where the LLM is only used for structured local relation judgment rather than unconstrained decision making. Specifically, after candidate skills are synthesized, each candidate first retrieves its top-k neighboring skills from the current SkillBank. The candidate-neighbor pairs are then compared along three structured dimensions: **when-to-use overlap**, **action-skeleton overlap**, and **failure/guardrail conflict**. These comparison results are converted into one of four governance actions: **ADD**, **UPDATE**, **DEPRECATE**, or **NOOP**. Finally, regression testing is applied before the operation is committed; if the proposed update degrades performance beyond the tolerance, the SkillBank is rolled back.

We will also add the following implementation table to make the engineering choices reproducible.

| Component | Implementation Choice | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Experience distillation | Multi-pass structured prompts for situation, observations, key steps, and failure boundaries | Convert raw trajectories into reusable experience objects |
| Experience clustering | Incremental embedding-similarity assignment | Group recurring experience patterns without reclustering all past data |
| Clustering threshold | 0.75 by default | Balance over-merging and over-fragmentation |
| Cluster maturity | Promote only clusters with sufficient support | Avoid synthesizing skills from isolated anecdotes |
| Skill synthesis | Multi-pass schema filling: principle, when-to-use, action skeleton, retrieval features, failure modes, guardrails | Produce structured reusable skills |
| Neighbor retrieval | Top-k nearest SkillBank entries | Restrict governance comparison to a local neighborhood |
| Governance comparison | Structured comparison over applicability, procedure, and conflict | Decide ADD / UPDATE / DEPRECATE / NOOP |
| Regression testing | Pre-update vs. post-update evaluation on a stratified subset | Reject harmful SkillBank updates |
| Rollback policy | Discard the proposed update if RegTest shows unstable degradation | Preserve SkillBank stability under continual growth |

This additional description clarifies that EvoSkillBank is not an ad-hoc collection of engineering heuristics. The key design is to constrain every stage with structured schemas and local decision rules: trajectories are compressed into experience objects, experience objects are clustered into recurring patterns, patterns are synthesized into schema-constrained skills, and candidate skills are admitted only through neighbor-based governance plus regression validation.

## Generalization

We also agree that evaluating only Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct was insufficient to support claims about generality. We therefore added experiments with four additional base models: **Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507**, **Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507**, **GPT-4o**, and **Gemini-2.5-Pro**. For each model, we compare ReAct and EvoSkillBank under the same setting.

For ReAct:

| Model | Pick | Look | Clean | Heat | Cool | Pick2 | ALFWorld Avg. | WebShop Score | WebShop Succ. |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | 44.7 | 32.8 | 31.5 | 12.1 | 16.9 | 15.3 | 25.6 | 43.8 | 17.6 |
| Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 | 67.4 | 52.8 | 18.7 | 36.5 | 22.1 | 27.6 | 37.5 | 47.6 | 15.9 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 | 79.6 | 58.4 | 39.7 | 49.1 | 31.8 | 61.2 | 53.3 | 42.5 | 13.2 |
| GPT-4o | 78.9 | 60.2 | 22.4 | 53.7 | 19.6 | 38.8 | 45.6 | 31.8 | 25.9 |
| Gemini-2.5-Pro | 82.6 | 50.9 | 63.8 | 65.1 | 27.4 | 56.7 | 57.8 | 50.4 | 36.5 |

For **EvoSkillBank**:

| Model | Pick | Look | Clean | Heat | Cool | Pick2 | ALFWorld Avg. | WebShop Score | WebShop Succ. |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | 72.8 | 64.9 | 47.6 | 39.8 | 35.4 | 30.1 | 48.4 | 61.7 | 31.5 |
| Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 | 75.9 | 58.7 | 51.6 | 53.9 | 63.8 | 38.4 | 57.1 | 50.2 | 35.7 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 | 80.7 | 75.6 | 77.9 | 80.8 | 59.6 | 55.9 | 71.8 | 57.2 | 54.9 |
| GPT-4o | 88.4 | 86.7 | 84.9 | 88.6 | 78.9 | 85.4 | 85.5 | 73.8 | 63.9 |
| Gemini-2.5-Pro | 92.7 | 91.8 | 88.6 | 84.9 | 74.8 | 91.9 | 87.5 | 80.9 | 70.8 |

Across all tested backbones, EvoSkillBank consistently improves over ReAct on the aggregate ALFWorld and WebShop metrics. This suggests that the method is not tied to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct specifically. Instead, the SkillBank functions as a model-agnostic test-time learning substrate that provides reusable procedural knowledge to different LLM workers, including both open-source and closed-source models.

summary.value: EvoSkillBank converts test-time trajectories into reusable skills through three stages (experience distillation, cross-episode clustering, skill synthesis) and governs skill bank updates via structured decisions (ADD/UPDATE/DEPRECATE/NOOP) with regression testing. Evaluated on ALFWorld, WebShop, and search-augmented QA, it achieves the best overall performance, with an additive ablation showing each component contributes incrementally.

reasons_to_reject.value:
1. Nearly every component relies on LLM-as-judge (6 distillation prompts, 4 synthesis passes, governance comparison, conflict detection, regression evaluation) with no ground-truth validation of accuracy.
2. Gains are modest (ALFWorld: 48.4% vs. 46.3% MemP; WebShop: 31.5% with several comparable baselines); governance adds only +4.6 and +3.3 over self-evolution alone on ALFWorld and WebShop.
3. Governance (w/o RegTest) hurts Hop QA performance vs. self-evolution alone (34.3 vs. 39.4 in Table 3), but this negative result is not discussed.
4. Key baselines are missing (SkillRL, Voyager), and ReAct/Reflexion/Mem0 results are copied from other papers with potentially different settings.
5. No analysis of how LLM cost grows with iterations or how retrieval latency scales with bank size.
6. Single base model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) throughout.
7. No analysis of sensitivity to the clustering threshold for incremental assignment; over-fragmentation or over-merging of skill clusters could degrade quality.
8. The regression testing uses a held-out subset $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{eval}}$, but its size, selection criteria, and risk of overfitting the SkillBank to this subset are not discussed.

reasons_to_accept.value:
1. The paper fills a real gap: existing work handles skill construction, retrieval, or invocation separately, but not end-to-end continual evolution with quality control.
2. The governance mechanism (structured relation judgment + neighbor retrieval + regression testing before commitment) addresses a practical concern about skill degradation during growth.
3. Detailed prompt templates (Prompts A-R) demonstrate careful multi-pass distillation design.
4. Evolution dynamics (Figure 2) and retrieval quality (Figure 3) analyses show the expected transition from rapid expansion to selective refinement.
5. Evaluation spans embodied, interactive, and knowledge-intensive domains.

questions_to_authors.value:
1. [Reject 1] Can you validate governance classification accuracy against human judgment? For example, on a subset of decisions, how often do humans agree with the LLM's ADD/UPDATE/DEPRECATE/NOOP labels?
2. [Reject 3] Why does governance (w/o RegTest) hurt Hop QA performance vs. self-evolution alone (34.3 vs. 39.4 in Table 3)?
3. [Reject 5] What is the total computational cost (LLM calls, tokens processed) for one full iteration of evolution + governance on each benchmark?
4. [Reject 6] Have you tested EvoSkillBank with a different base model (e.g., a larger model or a different family)? How much of the improvement is tied to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct specifically?
5. [Reject 7] How sensitive is the framework to the clustering threshold? Is there a risk of over-fragmentation or over-merging?

abstract.value: Agent skills are a natural substrate for continual learning in large language model agents because they allow useful procedural knowledge to be loaded only when needed rather than kept in context at all times, which support progressive disclosure of external experience and tools. However,  practical skill learning still faces two coupled challenges: skills must keep evolving from execution-time experience to adapt to tasks, and, once large numbers of new skills are appended, there is no effective governance mechanism that respects the unique properties of skills as reusable procedural objects. In this paper, we introduce **EvoSkillBank**, a controlled continual skill learning framework that enables agents to self-evolve skills from benchmark interaction traces while maintaining a persistent and governed SkillBank. EvoSkillBank combines a test-time self-evolution process for turning raw trajectories into reusable skill candidates with a SkillBank evolution framework that regulates how newly generated skills are added, merged, deprecated, or rejected. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, QA show that EvoSkillBank consistently improves over direct inference and static skill repositories, while yielding a compact and increasingly stable SkillBank under continual growth. We release the repository for both our self-evolution framework and the governed skill storage system to support future research on controlled continual skill learning for agentic LLMs.
